t: Introduction to the topic and aim of the session
n: In this lecture we study the examination of the body of a newborn. Examination of the body of a newborn is carried out when there are signs of violent death or suspicion of it, and special, specific questions are posed in it. In forensic medicine the newborn period means the first 24 hours; in paediatrics this period is 4 weeks, and in obstetrics 7 days. Plan of the lecture: signs of the newborn state, tests for live birth, gestational age, viability, duration of life, care, and causes of death. Attention: do not confuse the 4-week neonatal period in paediatrics with the forensic medical 24-hour period. This difference is related to the requirements of the law.

t: Cases in which examination is carried out
n: We consider the cases in which examination is carried out. First, examination is ordered when the body of a newborn whose mother is unknown is found. Second, examination is also carried out in cases of stillbirth in a delivery that took place outside a medical institution. Third, examination is also carried out when there is a complaint about the medical care given to a pregnant woman. Besides the special questions, the cause and time of death, the injuries and the mechanism of their infliction are also determined.

t: Special questions resolved by the examination
n: We consider in order the special questions resolved by the examination. First the question is posed whether the infant is newborn. Then it is determined whether it was born alive, after which the gestational age and viability are established. It is also checked how long the infant lived and whether it was cared for. In addition to these questions, the cause of death, the time of death and the mechanism of injury are determined. The question of live birth is resolved mainly by whether the infant breathed. Attention: the concepts “newborn” and “born alive” are not the same; they are separate questions.

t: General questions: cause of death and injuries
n: We speak about the general questions. In examination of the body of a newborn, in addition to the special questions, the cause and time of death are determined, as in other examinations of a corpse. The presence or absence of bodily injuries and the mechanism of their infliction are also among the questions put to the examination. The examination is carried out when the body of a newborn whose mother is unknown is found, in stillbirth outside a medical institution, or when there is a complaint about medical care. Remember: the special questions, that is, the newborn state, live birth, care and the like, supplement the general questions but do not replace them.

t: Newborn state: the view of three sciences
n: We consider the newborn state from the viewpoint of three sciences. In forensic medicine the concept of the newborn state differs from that in paediatrics and in obstetrics and gynaecology. In paediatrics the neonatal period is 4 weeks, in obstetrics and gynaecology 7 days, and in forensic medicine 24 hours. This difference is closely related to legislative requirements, so forensic medicine takes the shortest period. Attention: the forensic medical newborn state, that is, 24 hours, is not equal to the paediatric neonatal period, that is, 4 weeks.

t: Legal significance of the newborn state
n: We consider the legal significance of the newborn state. In the Criminal Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan, the intentional killing by a mother of her infant during delivery or immediately after birth is singled out separately in Article 99. The penalty under this article is set considerably milder than for intentional homicide. Labour lasts about a day; because of pain and her psycho-emotional state, the mother may inflict injury on the infant without fully realising it. Attention: if the same act is committed by another person, it is assessed as intentional homicide, that is, Article 97. Do not confuse Article 99 and Article 97.

t: Quick question: the concept of the newborn state
n: We consolidate with quick questions. First question: how long does the newborn period last in forensic medicine? Answer: the first 24 hours after birth. Second question: and in paediatrics and obstetrics? Answer: in paediatrics 4 weeks, that is, the neonatal period, in obstetrics 7 days. Third question: which article applies if a mother kills her infant during delivery or immediately after birth? Answer: Article 99 of the Criminal Code, with a milder penalty. Attention, there is a risk of error: 24 hours, 7 days and 4 weeks are not equal to one another. If another person kills the infant, it is assessed under Article 97, that is, as intentional homicide.

t: Signs of the newborn state: general description
n: We consider the general description of the signs of the newborn state. The signs: traces of blood on the body, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum, meconium, the state of the umbilical cord and primary atelectasis of the lungs. There are three absolute signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence or initial signs of the demarcation ring on the umbilical cord, and an unseparated umbilical cord. Traces of blood, vernix, swelling and meconium are relative signs. Attention: finding a relative sign does not absolutely prove that the infant is indeed newborn. Only the absolute signs are reliable.

t: Traces of blood on the body
n: We consider traces of blood on the body. In the absence of external injury, finding traces of blood on the body is regarded as a sign of the newborn state. Traces of blood arise from tears and cracks of the soft tissues of the birth canal. If the infant's body has been washed after birth, the traces of blood disappear. Cleanness from traces of blood and vernix indicates that the infant was cared for. This is important for the question of care.

We speak about vernix caseosa. The body of a newborn is covered with a whitish-grey, semi-fluid, semi-solid, cheese-like mass. It contains the secretion of the sebaceous glands of the skin, which function from the 5th month of intrauterine life; also desquamated epidermal cells, lanugo hairs and amniotic fluid. Its function is that, inside the uterus, it protects the fetal skin from maceration by the amniotic fluid, that is, from softening of the skin. There is especially a lot of it in skin folds, in the axillae and in the perineum, and it persists for a long time; if not washed off, it may remain for up to a week.

We consider caput succedaneum. In labour the presenting part of the fetal body is compressed in the pelvic ring. The local circulation is disturbed and the soft tissues swell. The swelling occurs mainly in a narrow pelvis and in weak labour from various causes. It is found more often in the region of the head, sometimes in the region of the buttocks. The consistency is soft, and on section a reddish-yellowish, that is, blood-stained serous, fluid emerges. Caput succedaneum usually resolves by itself within 2-3 days.

t: Difference between caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma
n: We consider the difference between caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma. Caput succedaneum does not respect the boundaries of the sutures, whereas cephalohaematoma is limited by the interosseous sutures. In caput succedaneum the tissue swells because of disturbed circulation; it is also found in the projection of the suture and is usually resorbed in 2-3 days. Cephalohaematoma forms in birth trauma from haemorrhage beneath the periosteum of the bones of the cranial vault; it lies over one or several bones and takes 2 weeks or more to resolve. Attention: caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma must be distinguished.

t: Attention: do not confuse the swelling with cephalohaematoma
n: Caput succedaneum and cephalohaematoma must not be confused. Caput succedaneum is oedema of soft tissues due to compression, in labour, of the presenting part of the fetal body in the pelvic ring. It is more often found on the head, sometimes on the buttocks. On section the oedema is reddish-yellow and usually resolves in 2-3 days; it is also found in the projection of the interosseous sutures. Cephalohaematoma forms from haemorrhage beneath the periosteum of the bones of the cranial vault; it lies on the bone and is limited by the sutures. Remember: oedema crosses the suture and resolves in 2-3 days, whereas cephalohaematoma is limited by the suture and resolves in more than 2 weeks.

We speak about meconium. Meconium, that is, the first stool, is a dark green or brownish-green, semi-fluid, uniform mass. It is found in the large intestine, around the anus, and in the region of the buttocks and thighs. It contains mucus, bile pigments, desquamated intestinal epithelium, amniotic fluid and lanugo hairs. Because its composition changes with the duration of pregnancy, it is used in determining fetal age. Usually meconium is completely passed from the intestine 1-2 days after birth; in premature infants this period is longer, up to 3-4 days.

We consider the structure and changes of the umbilical cord. The umbilical cord connects the fetus with the placenta. In a full-term infant it is 50-60 cm long and 1.5-2 cm thick. In live birth the cord dries evenly, and a reddish rim, that is, the demarcation ring, appears at its base. The chain of changes is as follows: first moist, shiny, whitish-reddish; then it dries and shrivels and takes on a brownish-yellow tint; within hours the demarcation ring appears; then a brownish-black colour; on days 5-7 the cord separates. Absence of the ring or its initial signs, and a cord not separated from the body and placenta, is an absolute sign.

We consider primary atelectasis of the lungs. A lung that has not breathed is in a state of primary atelectasis. Such an infant can live only a few seconds. Macroscopically the lungs are small in volume, dense, and located close to the spine; the surface is smooth, bluish-dark red. The weight of lungs that have not breathed is 55-60 g; after inspiration the circulation begins and the weight reaches 85-90 g. The specific gravity of a lung that has not breathed is 1.05-1.06, and of one that has breathed is below 1.0; a lung that has not breathed sinks in water. Attention: primary and secondary atelectasis are not the same. In secondary atelectasis the lungs first breathed and then collapsed again.

We compare absolute and relative signs. An absolute sign is regarded as unconditionally reliable: it precisely proves the newborn state. These are primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence or onset of the demarcation ring, and a cord not separated from the body and placenta. Traces of blood, vernix, swelling and meconium are relative signs. Relative signs may also be found on the second and subsequent days of the infant's life. Attention: vernix, if not washed off, persists for up to a week, so it cannot be the sole proof.

t: Case analysis: signs of the newborn state
n: Case analysis: signs of the newborn state. The body of a newborn whose mother is unknown was found. The umbilical cord is not separated from the placenta, and there are vernix and traces of blood on the body. On internal examination the chest is flat, the lungs are small, dense and bluish-dark red; in the water test the lungs sink. Question: is this infant newborn, and was it born alive? Which signs are absolute and which relative? Guidance: an unseparated cord and primary atelectasis are absolute signs. If the test is negative, also exclude secondary atelectasis.

We consider the criteria of live birth. According to the WHO recommendation, the criteria of live birth are: breathing outside the mother's body, heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation or voluntary movements. In forensic medicine, methods of determining heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation and voluntary movements after death have not yet been developed. Therefore the question of live birth is resolved mainly by establishing whether the infant breathed or not. Tests and microscopic examinations are used for this. Attention: live birth and viability are not the same; an infant born alive may in some cases be non-viable.

We consider the lung test, that is, the Galen-Rauger-Schreyer test. The test was first used in forensic practice by J. Schreyer in 1681. First ligatures are placed on the complex of thoracic organs, then the complex is placed in a vessel of water. If pieces of lung sink, the result is assessed at that point; with a positive result the test is stopped. The specific gravity of a lung that has not breathed is 1.05-1.06, that is, greater than water, so it sinks. In a lung that has breathed, because of the air, the specific gravity is below 1.0 and the lung floats.

t: False results of the lung test
n: We consider false results of the lung test. A false positive result may occur in putrefied bodies, with artificial respiration, and in frozen lungs that have thawed poorly. Pieces that have risen because of putrefactive gas do not rise again when compressed under water; a fully thawed frozen lung sinks. A false negative result occurs in secondary atelectasis: a lung that previously breathed undergoes atelectasis because of inflammation or airway obstruction. In this case the Taranukhin method (1907) or the Trakhtenberg modification (1958) is used: the piece floats to the surface of the water in a flask under reduced pressure.

We consider the Taranukhin method and its modification. In secondary atelectasis, a lung that previously breathed becomes airless again because of inflammation or airway obstruction. The ordinary lung test may give a false negative result; therefore the method of V. Taranukhin (1907) or the modification of L.Ya. Trakhtenberg (1958) is recommended. If a piece that sank at ordinary pressure floats to the surface of the water at reduced pressure, air has remained in it. This indicates secondary atelectasis.

We consider the gastrointestinal test, that is, the Breslau test. The test is associated with the name of V. Breslau (1865). It is based on the fact that, in breathing, part of the air passes through the oesophagus into the stomach and intestines. Ligatures are placed at the entrance and exit of the stomach, on the sections of intestine where air is suspected, and on the rectum. The organs are separated from the mesentery and placed in a vessel of water. Air-containing areas float, and when punctured, air bubbles emerge. Because the air passes gradually, the test is also useful for assessing the duration of life. Limitation: putrefactive gases and artificial ventilation of the lungs give a false positive result; in such cases use of the test is not recommended.

We consider the radiological test. The test is based on determining, before opening the body, the presence of air in the lungs, stomach and intestines. It was proposed in 1939 by Ya.G. Dillon. The main shortcoming is that radiography cannot distinguish a lung that has breathed from one that has been artificially ventilated or from the presence of putrefactive gases. In addition, special equipment is needed, and the diagnostic capability is limited. Therefore it is not now used in the practice of forensic medical examination.

Quick questions on the tests. First question: does a lung that has not breathed float or sink in water? Its specific gravity is 1.05-1.06, that is, greater than water; in one that has breathed it is below 1.0. Second question: in which cases may the lung test be false positive? In a putrefied body, with artificial respiration, and in a frozen lung that has thawed poorly. Third question: how do we distinguish putrefactive gas from respiratory air? When squeezed by hand under water, a piece with putrefactive gas does not rise again. Attention: false positive and false negative results are not the same. In secondary atelectasis the result is false negative; by the Taranukhin method the piece floats to the surface of the water at reduced pressure.

t: Macroscopic signs: lung that has breathed and one that has not
n: We compare the macroscopic signs of a lung that has breathed and one that has not. A lung that has breathed almost fills the chest and is elastic; on compression, frothy blood is released from the cut surface. The chest is barrel-shaped, the diaphragm is at the level of the 6th-7th rib, the surface is marbled, and the weight is 85-90 g. A lung that has not breathed is small, denser and lies close to the spine; on compression, less blood is released from the cut surface. The chest is flat, the diaphragm is at the level of the 4th-5th rib, the colour is uniform bluish-dark red, and the weight is 55-60 g. In live birth putrefaction begins from the respiratory organs, and in stillbirth usually from the region of the natural orifices.

We consider the microscopic signs. In stillbirth the alveoli are not expanded, the epithelium is cuboidal and the septa are thick. The elastic fibres are bundle-like and there is no blood in the capillaries. In a lung that has breathed, the alveoli are expanded, the epithelium is flat and the septa are thin. The capillaries are congested and the elastic fibres are arranged in order. Hyaline membranes, that is, albumin, globulin and fibrin, are found mainly in premature infants born alive and living several hours; in the absence of breathing they are not present.

Case analysis: establishing live birth. In the putrefied body of a newborn, pieces of lung floated to the surface of the water. Does this prove that the infant was born alive? Putrefactive gases may give a false positive result of the lung test; artificial respiration and a poorly thawed frozen lung also give such a result. The method of distinguishing: the floating piece is squeezed by hand under water. A piece that has risen because of gas does not float up to the surface again. Attention, there is a risk of error: in putrefaction or artificial respiration the gastrointestinal test also gives a false positive result, so it is not recommended.

t: Concepts of full term and maturity
n: We consider the concepts of full term and maturity. Full term is a set of signs indicating that pregnancy lasted on average 10 lunar months, or 280 days. According to the World Health Organization, delivery at 37-42 weeks is regarded as timely. A full-term infant's length is on average 50-54 cm and weight 3000-3500 g. Maturity is physical development sufficient for life outside the mother's body: body length 45 cm and more, and weight not less than 2500 g. An infant shorter than 25 cm or weighing less than 500 g is non-viable, and its body is not opened. Attention: full term and maturity are not the same. For the investigating authorities they are important in resolving questions of the duration of pregnancy and viability.

We consider determining gestational age by formulae. Haase's formula gives age in lunar months, and the calculation is done differently in the first and second halves of pregnancy. In the first half the square root of the body length is taken, for example with 16 cm it gives 4 months. In the second half the body length is divided by 5, for example with 40 cm it gives 8 months. The Baltazard-Dervieux index is 5.6; it is multiplied by the body length and the age is found in days, for example 40 multiplied by 5.6 gives 224 days, that is, 8 months. In Yakupov's method the head circumference is divided by 3.4 and the result gives lunar months; for example with 34 cm it gives 10 months.

t: Umbilical cord, placenta and ossification centres
n: We consider the umbilical cord, placenta and ossification centres. As the month of pregnancy increases, the length of the cord and the mass of the placenta increase; selected months are given in the table. At month VI the cord is 38 cm and the placenta 250 g; at VII, 42 cm and 340 g; at VIII, 46 cm and 410 g; at X, 50 cm and 500 g. The ossification centre appears in the calcaneus in month V, in the talus in month VII, and in the lower femoral epiphysis, that is, the Béclard nucleus, in month IX. The swallowing reflex appears in the 8th lunar month; therefore lanugo hairs are found in the meconium.

We consider viability. Viability is the infant's ability to live outside the mother's body. An infant born alive may also be non-viable. The criterion of the World Health Organization: an infant shorter than 25 cm and weighing less than 500 g is non-viable because of extreme prematurity. The body of such an infant is not opened: only an external examination is carried out, and the weight and length are measured. Defects incompatible with life: anencephaly, a two-chambered heart. If there is an external defect, for example a sixth finger or cleft lip, the internal defects are also examined. Birth trauma also removes viability: disproportionate injuries such as crushing of the brain, or fracture of the cervical vertebrae with injury to the spinal cord.

t: Case analysis: full term and viability
n: Case analysis, a teaching example: an infant born alive was found, body length 24 cm, weight 480 g. How is its viability assessed? By the WHO criterion, the length is less than 25 cm and the weight less than 500 g, so because of extreme prematurity the infant is non-viable and its body is not opened. Compare: a full-term infant is born at 37-42 weeks, 50-54 cm, 3000-3500 g. A mature infant is at least 45 cm and 2500 g. Attention: full term, maturity and viability are not the same; these three concepts are assessed separately. Question: why are weight and length taken together?

t: Duration of life outside the mother's body
n: We consider the assessment of the duration of life outside the mother's body. Caput succedaneum resolves on days 2-3; neonatal jaundice appears on days 2-3 and passes on days 1-10. Air fills the small intestine in 5-6 hours and passes into the large intestine after 6 hours. Hyaline membranes are found in the pulmonary alveoli after not less than 1-2 hours. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. Secondary atelectasis of the lungs appears after not less than 5-6 hours. The demarcation ring on the cord and meconium correspond to the end of the first day. Attention: the time limits are approximate; the expert draws a conclusion taking into account as many signs as possible.

We consider establishing care of the infant. Establishing whether there was care is of great importance for the inquiry and the investigation in the legal assessment of the case. Signs of care: the infant is swaddled, clothing is on it, and the cord is cut and tied. If the body has been cleaned of traces of blood and vernix, this too indicates that the infant was cared for. On internal examination, finding milk or a similar mass in the stomach indicates care after birth.

t: Causes of death of the fetus and newborn: antenatal and intranatal
n: We consider the causes of death of the fetus and newborn: antenatal and intranatal. Antenatal non-violent death is most often due to intrauterine asphyxia: placenta praevia, infarction, abruption; compression of the cord, entanglement around the neck, a true knot; also aspiration of amniotic fluid and meconium. Intranatal death is mainly due to birth trauma: in a narrow pelvis, a large fetus or weak labour, the head is compressed, the skull bones are fractured, and intracranial haemorrhage occurs. In birth trauma there are no external injuries or wounds. If the mother helped with her hands, there are abrasions and bruises on the face and neck and a tear of the corner of the mouth.

We distinguish the active and passive kinds of infanticide. Violent death occurs mainly in the postnatal period, that is, after delivery; active and passive infanticide are distinguished. In the active kind, action is directed against the infant: strangulation by hand or ligature, drowning, mechanical injury, throwing into fire. In the passive kind, the infant is left without care: hypothermia, starvation; if the cord is not tied, external bleeding. Causes of non-violent death: extreme prematurity, defects incompatible with life, haemolytic disease. Attention: active and passive are not the same. For law enforcement bodies the precise cause of death is important, not the kind.

We consider the features of conducting the examination. The first stage is external examination: the swaddling and clothing are inspected, the length, weight, and the circumferences of head, chest and shoulders are measured, and traces of blood, vernix, caput succedaneum, meconium and defects are assessed. The second stage is internal examination; it begins with the chest and abdominal cavities, in the oral cavity the median incision begins from the lower lip, and the integrity of the umbilical vessels is preserved. In the cranial cavity the bones are cut with scissors and windows are opened in the cranial vault so that the falx, sinuses and tentorium cerebelli remain intact. For live birth, flotation tests of the lungs and gastrointestinal tract are carried out. For histology and blood group, a piece is also taken from the placenta and umbilical cord.

Let us sum up. Absolute, that is, unconditionally reliable, signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence or initial signs of the demarcation ring, an unseparated umbilical cord. Full term: delivery at 37-42 weeks, length 50-54 cm, weight 3000-3500 g. An infant shorter than 25 cm and weighing less than 500 g is non-viable. Review questions: what are the questions of the examination? What is the difference in the newborn state? Which signs are absolute? What is a false positive lung test and secondary atelectasis?
